drainage.local_h: Where the water goes in Carthage: sand on top, clay that stops it
local: Carthage ground is the classic East Texas stack. Sandy loam on top lets rain disappear fast, then it meets red clay and stops. From there the water has one place to go, and that is sideways, toward the slab, the low corner of the yard or the neighbor's fence. That is why a Carthage yard can be dust dry on the surface and still hold a pond after a long rain. We want to watch the water during or right after a storm when we can.

Half the yards we are called to for a French drain need something simpler. Roof water dumping at the foundation gets rerouted in solid pipe. Pine needles in the gutters make that worse by sending overflow down the wall. Ground that tips back toward the house is regraded to fall about six inches over the first ten feet. Small fixes like these run about $450 to $1,000, and they often solve the problem.

When water is already in the ground, a spongy spot that stays soft for days, we build a French drain once. Sock-wrapped 4-inch perforated pipe goes over 4 inches of #57 stone, backfilled with the same stone, with a steady fall to a daylighted outlet or a pop-up emitter. Cheap corrugated pipe laid shallow silts up in the clay in a season or two. A standard single run is about $1,900 to $3,000, and full systems run $3,000 to $4,500.

Outlet is the question on every lot. A yard with an acre or more, out toward Lake Murvaul, Beckville or Gary, often has a lower edge where the water can leave. A close-set in-town lot behind the courthouse square may need a pop-up emitter. We tell you on the walkthrough where it can go. Most Carthage projects land between $2,000 and $3,750, and spring is when soggy yards show up, so tell us before the rains.

faq.q: What does a French drain cost in Carthage?
faq.a: Small fixes like a downspout reroute run about $450 to $1,000. A standard single run is about $1,900 to $3,000, and full systems run $3,000 to $4,500. Most projects land between $2,000 and $3,750, depending on pipe length, depth and the outlet.

faq.q: Why does my yard hold water after every rain?
faq.a: Sandy topsoil over red clay lets water soak in fast and then stall on the clay, so it spreads sideways toward the slab or the low corner. We find where the water starts and where it can leave, then price the right fix.

faq.q: Do I really need a French drain?
faq.a: Maybe not. Most soggy yards are fed by surface water, such as roof runoff or a slope that tips toward the house. Those get fixed with downspout reroutes and regrading, for less money. A French drain is for water already in the ground, like a spot that stays spongy for days.

faq.q: Can you fix water pooling against my foundation?
faq.a: Yes. The ground should drop about six inches over the first ten feet out from the house. On older homes it has often settled the wrong way. We regrade to restore that fall, shape a swale to carry water around the house and reroute downspouts in solid pipe to a real outlet.

faq.q: When is the best time to look at a drainage problem?
faq.a: During or right after a rain, when the water shows us its path. Digging goes faster in a dry stretch, because saturated clay is heavy. Getting it done before spring rains means no more seasons with a pond in the back corner.

fertilization.local_h: A fertilizer plan for sandy topsoil and a yard split between shade and sun
local: Sandy loam sits on top in most Carthage lots, and sand lets nutrients wash down and out of reach fast. A big dose in one visit mostly feeds the next rainstorm. That is why we use slow-release fertilizer and split the year into four feedings instead of one heavy one. It also explains why a soil test comes first. We would rather read the numbers than assume your yard matches the bag.

A lot of Carthage yards have St. Augustine under mature trees in front and Bermuda in the open behind. Those two do not eat the same. Shaded St. Augustine grows slowly and uses less, so pushing it hard only makes soft growth. Sunny Bermuda can take more. We set the rate area by area and write it into the plan, so the front and back of the same yard are not treated as one number.

Most East Texas soil runs a little acidic, and years of loblolly needles add to it. If the test shows low pH, we correct it with lime, and that can matter as much as the fertilizer itself. The first feeding goes down around April 25, once nights hold above 60 degrees. The last real nitrogen goes on in the first two weeks of September, and October is a potassium month, not a nitrogen month.

Red clay underneath the sand packs down on lawns that see traffic, and a compacted lawn sheds water instead of drinking it. For those yards we add core aeration in late August through mid-September, with the feeding right behind it. On an acre or more outside town, we feed the maintained lawn around the house, and the plan and price come in writing before the first application. No weed or pest products are part of the program.

faq.q: Should I feed shady St. Augustine as much as sunny Bermuda?
faq.a: No. Grass in shade uses less, and heavy feeding on shaded St. Augustine mostly grows soft blades. Sunny Bermuda can take more. We set the rate by area, so the front and back of one Carthage yard each get what they can use.

faq.q: When does the first fertilizer go down in Carthage?
faq.a: Around April 25, once nights hold above 60 degrees and the grass is fully awake. Feeding in March mostly washes out with the next rain, because Bermuda and St. Augustine are still half dormant and cannot take it up, and sandy topsoil lets it leave even faster.

faq.q: What does lawn fertilization cost in Carthage?
faq.a: Visits start from about $190. A full seasonal program depends on lawn size and the number of rounds, usually four. You get the plan and price in writing before the first application, and lime or aeration is quoted with it.

faq.q: Does the program include weed or pest treatments?
faq.a: No. We do not apply weed, insect or disease products. The program is soil testing, fertilizer, lime when the test calls for it, core aeration and a fall winterizer. The goal is a fed, well-rooted lawn.

faq.q: Do you aerate clay lawns in Carthage?
faq.a: Yes, with core aeration that pulls plugs out of the ground, not spikes that shove clay sideways and pack it tighter. The window is late August through mid-September while the grass can still heal the holes. Water the day before so the tines do not skip on dry ground.

flower-bed-installation.local_h: Two kinds of bed in Carthage: baked in sun or buried in pine shade
local: Carthage beds fall into two camps. On open lots, a bed facing west bakes in afternoon sun from June through September. Under the pines on older streets, a bed sees a few hours of light at best and gets needles all year. One plant list cannot cover both. So the first thing we do on a walkthrough is count hours of sun and watch where water goes after a rain, then draw the bed to match what the spot can support.

For hot beds, lantana, salvia, plumbago and knockout roses carry through July and August. Annual vinca joins them, but not before mid-May, since a cool, wet spring rots it. For shade beds, azaleas and hollies like the acidic soil the pine needles leave behind. Spring annuals like petunias and impatiens look good in April and are crisp by July, so they are not the backbone of any bed we plant here.

Most beds fail because of what is under them, not what is in them. Sandy topsoil over red clay means water either races through or stalls on the clay. We loosen the top, work compost into the heavy spots and set a grade that moves water off, so roots never sit wet. We pull every weed by the root, and we put no landscape fabric under the mulch. Mulch goes down at 1 to 1.5 inches, pulled back off every stem.

Edging comes in stone, steel or a natural cut, and the type changes the price along with plant count, plant size and soil prep. If you want to see the bed before we dig, the $199 Flower Bed Preview gives you a rendering, a plant list and the edging spec, credited toward an install within 90 days. Shrubs and perennials do best planted in fall. Watering advice is simple: deep and less often, because daily watering drowns roots in clay.

faq.q: What flowers survive a Carthage summer?
faq.a: In full sun, lantana, annual vinca, salvia, plumbago and knockout roses hold up through July and August. They want sun and good drainage and dislike wet roots. In pine shade, azaleas and hollies are the dependable choice, since they like acidic soil. Vinca waits until mid-May, when the soil is truly warm.

faq.q: How much does a new flower bed cost in Carthage?
faq.a: Flower beds fall under our landscaping and planting work, where most projects run $900 to $3,600. A small refresh of an existing bed starts at a few hundred dollars. Bed size, plant count, edging and soil prep set the price.

faq.q: Why do beds under pines struggle?
faq.a: Low light and a steady fall of needles. The answer is plants that accept shade and acidic soil, such as azaleas and hollies, plus a bed built to drain. We also keep the mulch off the stems so the crowns can breathe.

faq.q: Do you put fabric under the mulch?
faq.a: No. Mulch breaks down into soil, and on top of fabric that soil becomes a seed bed. Weeds root through the sheet within a few years. We edge clean, prep the soil and mulch at the right depth. Fabric belongs under rock.

faq.q: How often should I water a new bed?
faq.a: Deep and less often. Daily light watering in clay keeps the roots wet and can kill good plants. We walk you through watering when the bed is done, and sandy spots that drain fast may need more water than the clay corners.

faq.q: How do you keep a patio from sinking in Carthage clay?

hedge-trimming.local_h: Bringing older Carthage foundation hedges back from boxes and bare legs
local: Walk the older streets near the courthouse square and you see the pattern. Hollies, ligustrum and boxwoods planted along the foundation years ago, then sheared flat on top and square on the sides every year. The top stays green and the bottom goes thin and bare, because light stops reaching the lower branches. We reshape them slightly wider at the base than at the top. It takes a season or two to fill back in, and the hedge stops looking like a box on stilts.

Timing matters as much as the cut. Hollies and boxwoods get their main shaping in early summer, after the spring flush hardens off, and June is the clean window. Azaleas get cut within a few weeks of finishing bloom, or you trim off next spring's flowers. We avoid hard cuts in August and later. Tender regrowth does not harden before the first freeze, and a brown hedge all winter is a bad trade for one early trim.

Pines drop needles all year in Carthage, and they love to lodge inside a hedge. Needles caught in the middle of a boxwood hold moisture and make the plant look worse than it is. Tarps go down before we start, and when we finish, the clippings and the needles are raked up, blown out of the beds and hauled off. Nothing is left in a pile for you to deal with.

A hedge that has been left for years may be past a gentle trim. Hard rejuvenation cuts take it back to a size it can grow into, and it looks rough for a season. Some plants handle that better than others. We tell you on the walkthrough which ones will come back and which are better replaced. A handful of foundation shrubs sits at the low end of the $150 to $800 range, and long rows run higher.

faq.q: When should hedges be trimmed in Carthage?
faq.a: Hollies, boxwoods and ligustrum get their main shaping in early summer, once the spring growth has hardened off. Azaleas are cut right after they bloom. We avoid hard cuts in late summer and fall, because new growth will not harden before the first freeze.

faq.q: How much does hedge trimming cost in Carthage?
faq.a: Most jobs run $150 to $800. A few foundation shrubs sit at the low end. Long rows, tall hedges or shrubs that have not been touched in years run higher. Hauling off clippings is part of the job, and the quote is itemized.

faq.q: My hedge is bare at the bottom. Can it be saved?
faq.a: Often, yes. We shape it wider at the base so light reaches the lower branches, and a hard cut can push new growth from old wood on plants that tolerate it. We tell you on the walkthrough if yours will come back or should be replaced.

faq.q: Do you clean the pine needles out of the hedge?
faq.a: Yes. Tarps go down first, and when we finish we rake and blow the needles and clippings out of the beds and haul everything away. Needles trapped inside the middle of a boxwood get cleared as part of the trim, so the plant can dry out and breathe again.

faq.q: Can you put the hedges on a recurring schedule?
faq.a: Yes. Most hedges want two to three trims between spring and fall. We can set a recurring schedule or come back when you call. Carthage is a longer run from Longview, so we go over scheduling on the first call.

irrigation.local_h: Watering a Carthage yard that runs sandy on top and clay below
local: The ground in Carthage is sandy loam over red clay, and a sprinkler schedule has to respect both. Sand takes water fast and dries fast. The clay under it stops the water and pushes it sideways. A system that runs one long cycle floods the low side of the yard and leaves the high side thirsty. Shorter cycles that let water soak in, with zones split by slope, keep the whole yard even.

Sun and shade drink differently, and Carthage lots often have both. St. Augustine in the shade under mature trees needs less water than Bermuda in the open, so they go on separate zones with their own run times. We lay out zones around how the yard actually behaves, with heads spaced for full coverage on turf. The goal is the right amount on each part and nothing on the driveway.

Beds under pines are the other half. Spray heads in a bed soak leaves, mulch and the siding and still leave roots thirsty. Drip puts water at the roots, wastes almost none and keeps foliage dry, which helps in a humid East Texas spring. A sprinkler system covers the yard around the house, not an open pasture. Outside town, water source and pressure can be different, so we check both on the walkthrough.

Texas treats irrigation as licensed work, and ours is done under a licensed irrigator, license LI0006657. Systems on city water need a backflow device, and new automatic systems need a rain or freeze sensor. Carthage is a longer run from Longview, so installs are scheduled as projects. Already have a system? We fix broken heads and lines, leaking valves, zones that will not come on and controllers nobody has set since the house was built.

faq.q: Do you install sprinkler systems in Carthage?
faq.a: Yes. We install and repair sprinkler systems in Carthage and around Panola County under a Texas licensed irrigator, license LI0006657, and we pull the permit the job requires. Installs are scheduled as projects because of the drive from Longview. The walkthrough and the written quote are both free.

faq.q: How much does a sprinkler system cost in Carthage?
faq.a: It depends on how much of the yard you want watered, how many zones that takes, whether the beds need drip, and your water source and pressure. We price irrigation after a free walkthrough instead of guessing from the street, and send a written, itemized quote, usually within a day.

faq.q: Do you repair systems you did not install?
faq.a: Yes. We fix broken heads and lines, leaking valves, bad wiring, zones that will not come on, heads that hit the street instead of the lawn, and controllers nobody has set in years. That includes systems we installed and systems someone else put in before you bought the house.

faq.q: Should my beds be on drip or spray?
faq.a: Drip, almost always. Spray heads in a bed wet the leaves, the mulch and the side of the house, and they waste water to wind and evaporation. Drip puts the water at the roots and keeps foliage dry, which helps keep fungus down in our humid springs, especially under pines.

faq.q: Does my sprinkler need a freeze sensor?
faq.a: New automatic systems need a rain or freeze sensor, and we install one. Before the first hard freeze, make sure the sensor works or shut the system off. When you turn it back on in spring, run every zone again and look for heads that sank, broke or point the wrong way.

mulch-installation.local_h: Pine straw, hardwood and the Carthage bed that already collects needles
local: Many Carthage lots already have loblolly pines overhead, and the beds under them collect needles for free. Pine straw makes a fine mulch on its own. It looks natural, knits together on a slope and breaks down slowly. For beds under pines, we can top-dress with pine straw and call it done. For a darker, finished look in front of the house, hardwood is the better choice, and we match whatever is already in the bed so it breaks down evenly.

Every online calculator says three inches. That number comes from places with snow loads. Three inches here sheds light rain like a tarp, holds moisture against stems until they rot and gives voles cover through winter. We lay 1 to 1.5 inches over a prepped bed. On sandy topsoil that is plenty to hold moisture, and a 2,000 square foot bed needs about 8 yards, not 19. We never lay fabric underneath.

Prep is the real work. We re-cut the bed edge so grass cannot creep in and pull every weed by the root, because mulch hides weeds and does not kill them. The crusted top inch of soil is loosened so rain reaches the roots. On larger beds out on an acre, we bring in bulk mulch by the yard so you pay for mulch and not bags, and use bagged mulch where the access is tight.

Two windows work well. Late April through mid-May comes right after the spring flush, before the heat. Late September through October is a thin fall top-dress ahead of the November leaf drop from the hardwoods. To check whether a bed needs more, push a finger through until you hit soil. If an inch is left, add an inch. Most Carthage bed refreshes run $600 to $2,400, and a thin top-dress costs a fraction of a full install.

faq.q: Is pine straw or hardwood mulch better in Carthage?
faq.a: Both work. Pine straw looks natural under pines and knits together on a slope. Hardwood gives a darker, finished look and builds the soil as it breaks down. Either way, we keep it at 1 to 1.5 inches and pull it back off plant stems.

faq.q: How much does mulch cost in Carthage?

faq.q: How deep should mulch be here?
faq.a: About 1 to 1.5 inches over a prepped bed. Anything much deeper sheds light rain like a tarp, holds moisture against stems until they rot and gives voles cover through the winter. Pull it back off stems and trunks, and do not put landscape fabric underneath. Fabric belongs under rock, not mulch.

faq.q: When is the best time to mulch in Carthage?
faq.a: Late April through mid-May, after the spring growth flush and before the heat, is the main window. Late September through October works for a thin top-dress before the hardwoods drop their leaves in November and the first cold front comes through. Pine straw can go down on the same schedule.

faq.q: Do you pull the weeds first?
faq.a: Yes, every weed comes out by the root before any mulch goes down. Mulch hides weeds but does not kill them, so the bed gets cleaned, the edge gets re-cut and the top inch of soil gets loosened first. That prep is most of what separates a good mulch job from a quick one.

retaining-walls.local_h: Why a modest Carthage slope can take out a bed or lean a fence
local: You do not need a hillside for a wall to matter in Carthage. A modest slope behind a house, after a few hard rains, can wash out a bed or push soil up against a fence line. Sandy topsoil moves easily, and the red clay below it stops water cold, so the water slides along the clay and carries the sand with it. A wall holds that grade in place and turns a sloped strip into flat ground you can use.

Water is what knocks walls over here. Clay holds water behind a wall, builds pressure and pushes the wall out until it leans. So every wall we build gets a gravel chimney and a perforated drain tied out to daylight or a pop-up emitter. The base matters too. Sandy loam over clay will not carry a wall set on undisturbed dirt, so we dig below grade, compact crushed stone and set the first course dead level.

Sometimes the answer is not a wall. If soil is washing because rain runs across the slope, a swale or French drain can fix it for less. If the grade itself is moving, or you want flat ground for a patio or a play area, that is a wall. We walk the slope, trace the water and tell you which one you need. Terraced walls step a steeper grade down in lower courses.

We build segmental block from Belgard and Pavestone for most yards, natural stone and boulder where the property suits it, and pressure-treated timber for some jobs. Walls over about four feet usually need engineered design and geogrid, and we tell you at the walkthrough if yours needs a stamped plan. faq.q: Why do retaining walls lean?
faq.a: Almost always water or a weak base. Clay holds water behind the wall until it pushes the wall out. A lean means the base or drainage is wrong, and propping it will not hold. A rebuild with a proper base and a drain is the real fix.

Where a spot gets under about four hours of sun, no grass lasts, and a shade bed or mulch is the honest answer. We tell you that before you buy.

Old turf and weeds come out to bare soil. Then we till two to three inches of compost or topsoil into the sandy loam, level and roll it. The red clay below the sand holds water, so low spots that stay soggy get a grading fix first, or the new sod sits wet and rots. Sod goes down tight with staggered seams over starter fertilizer. On a long rural drive, pallet access is one of the price factors, and we look at it on the walkthrough.

Watering decides whether a new install lives. Sand dries quickly, so new sod needs a deep morning soak every day for the first two weeks, then a taper to two deep soaks a week. Evening watering keeps blades wet all night and invites fungus. You get that schedule in writing. Bermuda goes down best from late April through August, St. Augustine from May through September. faq.q: Should my Carthage yard be Bermuda or St. Augustine?
faq.a: That comes down to sun. Bermuda needs six to eight hours of direct sun and takes heavy traffic. St. Augustine grows on about four to six hours and handles pine and oak shade. Many yards here need both, and we map the sun before we order anything.

faq.q: How much does sod cost in Carthage?

faq.q: Why did the sod in my shady yard die?
faq.a: Most often the grass did not match the light. Bermuda in a shaded yard thins to dirt by August no matter how it is fed. Under about four hours of sun nothing lasts, so those spots are better as a shade bed. We check the sun before we recommend a grass.

faq.q: How often do I water new sod?
faq.a: Every morning for about two weeks, deep enough to soak through the sod into the soil, until the roots grab. After that, two deep waterings a week that finish around sunrise. Sandy topsoil dries fast, so do not skip days in July heat.

faq.q: When is the best time to lay sod in Carthage?
faq.a: Bermuda goes down best from late April through August. St. Augustine does well from May through September and needs four to six weeks of root growth before dormancy, so get it in by the end of September. Sod laid in November just sits on the ground like a rug.

tree-planting.local_h: Where the shade tree goes on a Carthage lot, and which one
local: On the open lots outside the old part of town, the single best tree is a shade tree on the west side of the house. It blocks the afternoon sun that bakes a Carthage summer. We walk the lot, note where the sun lands, where the drive and power lines run and how far the tree will spread, and mark a spot that works in twenty years and not just this spring. A tree that has to be cut back to fit later was planted in the wrong place.

For this part of Panola County we lean on live oak, Shumard oak, southern magnolia and redbud. Bald cypress goes in the wetter spots, which is useful where the red clay holds water after a long rain. Crepe myrtles are sized to the space, since a Natchez wants 25 to 30 feet and an Acoma stays near 10. We skip Midwest maples and cool-climate fruit trees, which struggle here.

The hole is two to three times as wide as the root ball and no deeper than the ball is tall. The root flare sits at grade or an inch above. Native sand and clay go back in, not a pocket of bagged soil, because that pocket holds water like a bathtub on clay. We cut circling roots, build a watering basin, and lay a wide mulch ring pulled back off the trunk. Stakes go in only on windy, exposed lots.

Sandy topsoil dries out quickly, and a container tree dries out even faster than the ground around it. In July the root ball can be dust dry while the clay six inches away is still moist. You get a written schedule that has you soaking the ball itself, not the yard. Fall is the best window, with the soil warm and the air cooling, though winter planting while the tree is dormant still gets roots going. Bigger installs get a 30-day check.

faq.q: What trees do well in Carthage?
faq.a: Live oak, Shumard oak, southern magnolia and redbud do well, bald cypress suits wetter spots, and crepe myrtles work when sized for the space. We look at sun, drainage and overhead room first, so nothing has to be cut back to fit later.

faq.q: Where should I plant a shade tree on my lot?
faq.a: Usually on the west side of the house, where it blocks afternoon sun. We also check the drive, utilities, the roofline and the tree's mature spread before picking the spot, since a tree planted too close to the house becomes a problem in a decade.

faq.q: How much does tree planting cost in Carthage?
faq.a: We quote after a free walkthrough instead of publishing a price. The species and size of the tree drive most of the cost, along with how many you plant and how easy the spot is to reach. The written quote includes the aftercare plan.

faq.q: Should I buy a big tree to get shade faster?
faq.a: Usually not. A smaller tree planted in fall roots in fast and tends to catch up with a larger one within a few years. Bigger trees cost more, need more water and take longer to establish. We size the tree to the spot and to how long you are willing to wait.

faq.q: When should I plant a tree in Carthage?
faq.a: Fall, from September until about Thanksgiving, is the best window. The soil stays warm while the air cools, so roots grow for months before summer. Spring planting works, but a spring tree needs more watering through its first summer, and sandy topsoil dries out quickly around a new root ball.

tree-shrub-care.local_h: One Carthage yard, five plants, five different pruning dates
local: A mature Carthage yard might have a crepe myrtle by the drive, azaleas along the porch, hollies at the corners and two or three big shade trees out back. None of them want to be cut at the same time. Crepe myrtles and knockout roses go in February, while dormant. Azaleas wait until right after bloom. Hollies and boxwoods get shaped in early summer. Oaks are left alone through spring and early summer. We run the work as a calendar, not a one-day sweep.

Crepe myrtles are the most common case here. Many have been topped to knuckles, which grows back taller on weaker wood. We take the opposite approach: thin the tree, remove crossing and rubbing branches, and limb it up so the bark shows. Recovering a topped tree takes two or three winters, and we come back each February to finish it. If the knuckles have rot in them, cutting the tree to the ground and regrowing the trunks can be the better call.

The big trees in town and the pines out toward Beckville and Gary carry dead lower limbs that shade the lawn and drop on the mower. We clear those with clean cuts at the branch collar. We do not take down large trees near the house, and we do not do stump work. Those need a tree service with different equipment, and we will say so on the walkthrough. We do remove small trees and shrubs that have died or outgrown their spot.

Cleanup is part of the job: limbs, trimmings and sawdust are raked up and hauled off before we leave. We can refresh the mulch around tree bases and feed trees and shrubs on a seasonal schedule. After a storm, we clear downed limbs and debris. There is no published price for this work, because a light shaping on a few shrubs is a different job than recovering a row of crepe myrtles. You get an itemized quote in writing.

faq.q: When should I prune my crepe myrtles in Carthage?
faq.a: February, while the tree is dormant and before the buds break. We take out suckers, crossing branches and dead twigs and thin the canopy. We do not top them. A crepe myrtle blooms on new wood without being cut back to knuckles.

faq.q: Can you fix a crepe myrtle that was topped?
faq.a: Usually. Each February we keep the two or three best shoots on each knuckle and cut the rest flush. After a few seasons the knuckles blend into the canopy. If the knuckles have rot, cutting to the ground and regrowing trunks may be better.

faq.q: Do you remove large trees or stumps?
faq.a: No. We remove small trees and shrubs, and we clear storm debris and downed limbs. Large trees near the house and stumps are jobs for a tree service with the right equipment, and we will tell you that on the walkthrough.

faq.q: How much does tree and shrub care cost in Carthage?
faq.a: We do not publish a price, because the work swings with the number of plants, their size and condition, and what each one needs. Shaping a few shrubs is a very different job from recovering a row of topped crepe myrtles. The walkthrough is free, and the quote comes in writing, itemized.

faq.q: When do you prune oaks?
faq.a: Not in spring or early summer, when beetles are active and oak wilt can spread through fresh cuts. We prune oaks in the dead of winter or in late summer, and we cut storm-broken limbs clean and seal the wound right away.
